num:zwei.tx: From Middle High German zwei, from Old High German zwei (neuter of zwēne). Compare Dutch twee, English two, twain. In Old High German, and still today in some dialects, distinct forms are used for the three grammatical genders. Zwei was originally the neuter form, now used for all genders. The Old High German masculine zwēne is found back in early modern German zween; the feminine zwō lives on in …

noun:Zeitgeist.tx: Zeit (“time”) + Geist (“ghost”), calque of Latin genius saeculī commonly attributed to Johann Gottfried Herder (1744–1803).

prep:zwischen.tx: From Old High German in zuiskēn, from Old High German zuiski, from Proto-West Germanic *twisk(ī), from Proto-Germanic *twiskaz (“twofold, double”), from Proto-Indo-European *dwís (“twice, doubly; in two”).

noun:Zabel.tx: From Middle High German zabel, from Old High German zabal (“board, playing-board, dice game”), from Latin tabula (“board”). Compare Old English tæfl (“playing-board; board game”) and Icelandic tafl.

verb:zahlen.tx: From Middle High German zaln, zalen, from Old High German zalōn, from Proto-West Germanic *talōn, from Proto-Germanic *talōną (“to tell, recount; to count, reckon”). Cognate with Bavarian zoin, English tale, Dutch talen, Swedish tala, Danish tal. Equivalent to Zahl + -en.

verb:zählen.tx: From Middle High German zel(e)n, zellen, from Old High German zellan, from Proto-West Germanic *talljan, from Proto-Germanic *taljaną. The modern long vowel continues the 2nd and 3rd persons singular of the present (where West Germanic gemination did not occur); it was reinforced also by the lengthened vowel in Zahl (Middle High German zale).

noun:Zahn.tx: PIE word *h₃dónts Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *h₃ed- Proto-Indo-European *-ónts Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts Proto-Germanic *tanþs Proto-West Germanic *tanþ Old High German zand Middle High German zan German Zahn From Middle High German zan, zant, from Old High German zan, zand, from Proto-West Germanic *tanþ, from Proto-Germanic *tanþs. The Old High German nominative zan alongside zand is …

verb:zerstören.tx: From Middle High German zerstören, from Old High German zistōren, zirstōren, from Proto-West Germanic *staurijan. Equivalent to zer- + stören.

adj:zierlich.tx: From Middle High German zierlich. Equivalent to Zier + -lich. For the semantic development from "decorative" to "petite, small", cf. klein.

prep:zu.tx: From a spelling merger of two interrelated adpreps: 1.) Middle High German ze, from Old High German za, zi, from Proto-Germanic *ta; and 2.) Middle High German zuo, from Old High German zuo, from Proto-West Germanic *tō, from Proto-Germanic *tō. A distinction between both words has widely been retained in dialects, and also to some degree in modern spoken German (see pronunciation section below). …

adv:zu.tx: From a spelling merger of two interrelated adpreps: 1.) Middle High German ze, from Old High German za, zi, from Proto-Germanic *ta; and 2.) Middle High German zuo, from Old High German zuo, from Proto-West Germanic *tō, from Proto-Germanic *tō. A distinction between both words has widely been retained in dialects, and also to some degree in modern spoken German (see pronunciation section below). …

adj:zu.tx: From a spelling merger of two interrelated adpreps: 1.) Middle High German ze, from Old High German za, zi, from Proto-Germanic *ta; and 2.) Middle High German zuo, from Old High German zuo, from Proto-West Germanic *tō, from Proto-Germanic *tō. A distinction between both words has widely been retained in dialects, and also to some degree in modern spoken German (see pronunciation section below). …

noun:Zucker.tx: From Middle High German zucker, from Old High German zuckar, from early Italian zucchero, from Arabic سُكَّر (sukkar), from Persian شکر (šakar), from Sanskrit शर्करा (śárkarā, “grit, gravel; ground or candied sugar”). Cognates include Czech cukr, Hungarian cukor and Dutch suiker.

adv:zurück.tx: Middle High German zerucke; zu- + Rücken; the former was zuo, zū, ze and the latter was rücke, rucke, rück, ruck, rügge, rugge in Middle High German. Cognate with Hunsrik zurick, Low German torüch and Dutch terug.

intj:zurück.tx: Middle High German zerucke; zu- + Rücken; the former was zuo, zū, ze and the latter was rücke, rucke, rück, ruck, rügge, rugge in Middle High German. Cognate with Hunsrik zurick, Low German torüch and Dutch terug.

adv:zuvor.tx: tzuvor, tzu vor (14th century); equivalent to zu + vor.

num:zwölf.tx: From Middle High German zwölf, zwolf, zwelf, zwelif, from Old High German zwelif, from an original *twelif, from Proto-Germanic *twalif. Compare Hunsrik zwellef, Dutch twaalf, English twelve, Norwegian and Danish tolv.

noun:Zeit.tx: Inherited from Middle High German zīt, from Old High German zīt, from Proto-West Germanic *tīdi, from Proto-Germanic *tīdiz, from Proto-Indo-European *dih₂tís, from *déh₂itis, from *deh₂y- + *-tis. Cognate with Low German Tiet, Tied, Dutch tijd, English tide, Danish tid, Norwegian tid, Swedish tid. Also cognate, more distantly, with English time.

noun:Zug.tx: From Middle High German zuc, zug, from Old High German zug, from Proto-West Germanic *tugi, from Proto-Germanic *tugiz, an abstract noun belonging to Proto-Germanic *teuhaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull, lead”). Cognate with Dutch teug, Low German Tog, Hunsrik Zugh, English tug, Old English tyġe. Related to and synchronically serving as the associated noun of ziehen (“to pull, to draw”).

num:zig.tx: From the terminal syllable -zig in numerals such as zwanzig (“twenty”), vierzig (“forty”), achtzig (“eighty”). Compare Dutch tig.

verb:zeigen.tx: From Middle High German zeigen, from Old High German zeigōn, intensive of zīhan, whence modern zeihen (“to blame”). Ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ-, whence also Zeichen, English teach. In Modern German, zeigen absorbed the synonymous but entirely unrelated Middle High German zöugen (cognate with Gothic ataugjan); therefore the spellings zäugen, zeugen also occurred.

verb:zagen.tx: From Middle High German zagen, from Old High German erzagēn, with further origin unclear. Often assumed to be from a hypothetical Old High German *aʒ-agēn and Proto-Germanic *at-agēn, with an incorrect separation of *at (“at”). *agēn (“fear”) would be related to Proto-Germanic *agaz (“fear, dread”) and thus be from Proto-Indo-European *h₂égʰos (“distress”) and Proto-Indo-European *h₂egʰ- (“to be …

noun:Zigeuner.tx: Middle High German Cigäwnär (mentioning, 1420s), compare Zeginer and Ziginer (15th century). Most likely from a Medieval Greek term meaning "untouchable"; compare the Modern Greek designations Τσιγγάνοι (Tsingánoi), Αθίγγανοι (Athínganoi). Cognate to Hungarian cigány and terms borrowed from it such as English tzigane, Portuguese cigano, French tzigane, Romanian țigan, and Russian цыга́н (cygán); …

noun:Zimmer.tx: From Middle High German zimber, from Old High German zimbar, from Proto-West Germanic *timr, from Proto-Germanic *timrą, from Proto-Indo-European *dem- (“build, house”) (see Proto-Indo-European *dṓm). Cognate with English timber, Swedish timmer (“timber”), and Dutch timmer (“building; construction; room”).

noun:Zorn.tx: From Middle High German zorn, Old High German zorn, from Proto-Germanic *turnaz (“anger, wrath”), from Proto-Indo-European *dr̥-nós (whence English tear), from *der- (“to flay, split, shatter”). Cognate with Dutch toorn and Old English torn.

noun:Zubehör.tx: 17th century, northern alteration of the above form, itself from Middle High German zuogehœr(d)e, under influence of the equivalent Middle Low German tôbehö̂re, literally “to-belongings”, thus “that which belongs to something else”. The northern behören for gehören see also in Behörde; compare Dutch behoren.

noun:Zelle.tx: From Middle High German zelle, from Old High German zella (9th century), from Ecclesiastical Latin cella. The cytological sense (17th c.) is a semantic loan from English cell (coined by Robert Hooke).

noun:Zahl.tx: From Middle High German zāle, from Old High German zala, from Proto-West Germanic *talu, from Proto-Germanic *talō, from Proto-Indo-European *dol- (“reckoning, calculation, fraud”), from Proto-Indo-European *del- (“to reckon, calculate”), cognate with Danish tal and Danish tale, Dutch taal, Low German Tahl, Hunsrik Zaal, English tale.

noun:Zar.tx: Borrowed from Russian царь (carʹ), from Proto-Slavic *cěsařь, from Proto-Germanic *kaisaraz, from Latin Caesar. Doublet of Kaiser and Cäsar.

noun:Zebra.tx: 17th century, from Portuguese zebra, from Old Galician-Portuguese enzebro, ezebra, azebra (“wild ass”), from earlier cebrario (882), ezebrario (897), from Vulgar Latin *eciferus, from Latin equiferus (“wild ass”). Neuter gender probably after Pferd (“horse”).

noun:Zeppelin.tx: Named after Ferdinand Adolf Heinrich August Graf von Zeppelin.

noun:Zeta.tx: Borrowed from Latin zeta and Ancient Greek ζῆτα (zêta). Doublet of Zett.

noun:Zither.tx: See late Middle High German zitterlein. From Old High German zithara, from Latin cithara, from Ancient Greek κιθάρα (kithára). See also Gitarre.

noun:Zombie.tx: Borrowed from English zombie, ultimately of Bantu origin.

noun:Zone.tx: Borrowed, partially via French zone, from Latin zona, from Ancient Greek ζώνη (zṓnē, “belt”).

noun:Zoo.tx: Originally a clipping of zoologischer Garten.

noun:Zucchini.tx: Borrowed from Italian zucchini, plural of zucchino.

noun:Zwieback.tx: From zwie- (“twice”) + backen (“bake”): twice-baked, a calque of Italian biscotto.

adv:zusammen.tx: From Middle High German zesamene, zesamne, zesamen (“together”), from Old High German zisamane (“together”). From zu- (“to”) + sammen (“together”) (in Modern German, sammen is only found in compounds), from Proto-West Germanic *saman, from Proto-Germanic *samanai (“together”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”). Cognate with Low German tosamen (“together”), Middle English tosamen …

adj:zusammen.tx: From Middle High German zesamene, zesamne, zesamen (“together”), from Old High German zisamane (“together”). From zu- (“to”) + sammen (“together”) (in Modern German, sammen is only found in compounds), from Proto-West Germanic *saman, from Proto-Germanic *samanai (“together”), from Proto-Indo-European *sem- (“together, one”). Cognate with Low German tosamen (“together”), Middle English tosamen …

noun:Zahnfee.tx: Zahn + Fee, calque of English tooth fairy.

noun:Zahnstocher.tx: Probably from Zahn (“tooth”) + stochen (“to pick; to stoke, stir”) + -er (agent suffix). The verb is the (now uncommon) simplex of stochern (“to pick, poke repeatedly”). Alternatively it could also be a haplology for *Zahnstocherer.

noun:Zehe.tx: From Middle High German zēhe, from Old High German zēha, from Proto-West Germanic *taihā, from Proto-Germanic *taihwǭ (“toe”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to point out”). Compare Dutch teen.

verb:zerlaufen.tx: From Middle High German zerloufen, from Old High German ziloufan, zihloufan. Equivalent to zer- + laufen.

verb:ziehen.tx: From Middle High German ziehen, from Old High German ziohan, from Proto-West Germanic *teuhan, from Proto-Germanic *teuhaną, from Proto-Indo-European *dewk- (“to pull, lead”). Cognate with Low German tehn, Gothic 𐍄𐌹𐌿𐌷𐌰𐌽 (tiuhan), Middle Dutch tīen, Old English tēon, Old Norse toga, West Frisian tsjen. Compare obsolete English tee (“to draw, lead, proceed”) and from the same root as English tie.

noun:Zink.tx: Probably related to Zinke (“point, prong”), from Old High German zint (“a jag, point”), from Proto-West Germanic *tind, from Proto-Germanic *tinduz, *tindaz (“prong, pinnacle”), from Proto-Indo-European *(e)dont- (“tooth, projection”). Cognate with Dutch tinne (“battlement”), German Zinne (“pinnacle, battlement”), Danish tinde (“pinnacle, battlement”), Swedish tinne (“tooth of a rake”), Icelandic …

noun:Zinn.tx: From Middle High German zin, from Old High German zin, from Proto-West Germanic *tin. Cognate with English tin.

noun:Zoni.tx: Zone (“zone”) + -i. Zone is short for Sowjetische Besatzungszone (“Soviet occupation zone”), the common West German name for the GDR before 1970 (and a colloquial name after it).

noun:Zwerg.tx: From Middle High German twërc, from Old High German twërc, from Proto-West Germanic *dwerg, from Proto-Germanic *dwergaz. The development Middle High German tw- > modern German zw- is regular. Compare Dutch dwerg, English dwarf, Low German Dwarg, Danish dværg.

noun:Zwiebel.tx: From Middle High German zwibel, zwibolle, from Old High German zwibollo, from Late Latin cēpulla, diminutive of Latin cēpa.

noun:Zecke.tx: From Middle High German zëcke, from Old High German cëcho, from Proto-West Germanic *tīkō (“tick”).

noun:Zelt.tx: From Middle High German zëlt, from Old High German zëlt, from Proto-West Germanic *teld, from Proto-Germanic *teldą. Compare Danish telt (whence English tilt + native teld from Old English teld), Middle Dutch telt, Old Norse tjald (“tent”) (whence Norwegian Bokmål tjeld).

verb:zittern.tx: From Middle High German zitern, zittern, from Old High German *zitarōn, zittarōn, from Proto-Germanic *titrōną. Cognate with Icelandic titra, English teeter (and possibly dither).

noun:Zitteraal.tx: 18th century, from zittern (“to tremble”) + Aal (“eel”), after older Zitterfisch (“electric ray, torpedo”, 16th c., now distinguished as Zitterrochen). Compare Dutch sidderaal.

num:zehn.tx: From Middle High German zehen, from Old High German zehan, from Proto-West Germanic and Proto-Germanic *tehun (“ten”), from Proto-Indo-European *déḱm̥ (“ten”). Compare Dutch tien, Low German teihn, English ten, Gothic 𐍄𐌰𐌹𐌷𐌿𐌽 (taihun).

num:zwanzig.tx: From Middle High German zweinzec, from Old High German zweinzug, from Proto-Germanic *twaintigaz, *twai tigiwiz. Cognate with Dutch twintig, West Frisian tweintich, English twenty, Danish tyve. The form zwanzig goes back to dialects that had early on lowered Middle High German -ei- to [aɪ̯] (especially Bavarian); elsewhere the contraction yielded zwenzig, which waned around 1700 along with the uncontracted zweinzig.

num:zwo.tx: Zwo was originally feminine of Early New High German zween m, but is now used as a variant of zwei without gender distinction. Compare, however, Luxembourgish zwou, which is still a feminine form of zwéin. The same is true of some German dialects, e.g. in Switzerland. It is inherited from the feminine numerals: Middle High German zwō f, from Old High German zwō f, from Proto-West Germanic twō f, …

noun:Zirbeldrüse.tx: From Zirbel (“pine”) + Drüse (“gland”), calque of Ancient Greek κωνάριον (kōnárion, “pineal gland”), from κῶνος (kônos, “pine cone”).

noun:Zapfen.tx: From Middle High German zapfe, from Old High German zapho, from Proto-West Germanic *tappō, from Proto-Germanic *tappô. Cognate to English tap; more there.

noun:Zaster.tx: Borrowed from Romani sáster (“iron”), from Sanskrit अस्त्र (astra, “missile weapon”).

noun:Zimt.tx: From late Middle High German zimet, from earlier zinemīn, zinment, from Latin cinnamon, cinnamomum, from Ancient Greek κιννάμωμον (kinnámōmon), later κίνναμον (kínnamon), according to Herodotus from Phoenician, cognate with Hebrew קִנָּמוֹן (qinnāmōn).

noun:Zicke.tx: From Middle High German zickīn, from Old High German zickīn (“kid”), from Proto-West Germanic *tikkīn. Cognate with English tick (“goat”).

noun:Zuber.tx: From Middle High German zuber, zūber, from Old High German zubar, zwibar. See also Eimer.

verb:zinken.tx: * Sense 1 was borrowed in the beginning of the 20th century from Rotwelsch, a cant or thieves' argot, in which its verb zinkenen is documented since the 19th century. * Sense 2 is probably derived from the Rotwelsch locution Zinken stecken “to drop a hint, to tip-off, to give a signal”.

noun:Zunge.tx: From Middle High German zunge, from Old High German zunga, from Proto-West Germanic *tungā, from Proto-Germanic *tungǭ; from Proto-Indo-European *dn̥ǵʰwéh₂s (“tongue”). Germanic Cognates include Old Saxon tunga, Low German Tung, Old Dutch tunga, Dutch tong, Old English tunge (Modern English tongue), West Frisian tonge, Old Norse tunga (> Swedish tunga, Faroese tunga, Norwegian tunge, Swedish …

noun:Zylinder.tx: Borrowed from Latin cylindrus, from Ancient Greek κῠ́λινδρος (kŭ́lindros).

noun:Zaum.tx: From Middle High German zoum, from Old High German zoum, from Proto-West Germanic *taum, from Proto-Germanic *taumaz. Cognate with Dutch toom, Swedish töm, English team; hence a doublet of Team.

noun:Zaun.tx: From Middle High German zūn, from Old High German zūn. Cognate e.g. with Dutch tuin, English town, Danish tun.

noun:Zeichen.tx: From Middle High German zeichen, from Old High German zeihhan (“sign, symbol”), from Proto-West Germanic *taikn, from Proto-Germanic *taikną, *taiknaz (“sign”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to show”). Doublet of Token. Cognate with Bavarian Zoachn, Alemannic German Zeiche, Dutch teken, Low German Teiken, English token, Danish tegn, Swedish tecken.

noun:Zwilling.tx: From Middle High German zwillinc, zwinelinc, from Old High German zwiniling from an original *twiniling, from Proto-Germanic *twinilingaz, from *twinaz + *-lingaz. By surface analysis, zwie- + -ling. Compare Dutch tweeling, English twinling, Danish tvilling. More at twin.

noun:Zweig.tx: From Middle High German zwīc, from Old High German zwīg, from Proto-Germanic *twīgą. Cognate with Dutch twijg, English twig. Compare the latter for more.

noun:Zange.tx: From Middle High German zange, from Old High German zanga, from Proto-West Germanic *tangu, from Proto-Germanic *tangō, derived from Proto-Indo-European *denḱ- (“to bite”). Cognate with Dutch tang, English tong, Icelandic töng. Non-Germanic cognates include Albanian darë (“tongs”), Ancient Greek δάκνειν (dáknein, “to bite”), Sanskrit दशति (daśati, “to bite”).

noun:Zoll.tx: From Middle High German zol, from Old High German zol, from Proto-Germanic *tullō (“what is counted or told”), for which see Proto-West Germanic *tolnu (“toll”) for more. Cognate with English toll.

noun:Ziegel.tx: Inherited from Middle High German ziegel, from Old High German ziegal, ziagala, ziagal, from Proto-West Germanic *tigulā.

noun:Zipfel.tx: From Middle High German zipfel, equivalent to Zipf + -el.

noun:Zitze.tx: From Middle High German zitze, ultimately of imitative origin (Lallwort). Doublet of Titte, related to English tit.

noun:Zeug.tx: From Middle High German ziuc (“stuff, gear”), from Old High German giziug, from Proto-West Germanic *teug, from Proto-Germanic *teugą. Compare Dutch tuig (“tool, gear”), Old Norse tygi (“gear”). More at toy.

noun:Ziege.tx: From Middle High German zige, from Old High German ziga, from Proto-West Germanic *tigā. Ziege was originally found in Franconian dialects alongside otherwise exclusive Geiß. In Middle High German times, it established itself in the colonial dialects (East Central German) and also conquered vast areas of Low German, where the borrowing Middle Low German sēge was predominant since at least the …

noun:Zopf.tx: From Middle High German zopf, from Old High German zoph (“lock”). Cognate to Dutch and English top. Doublet of Topp

noun:Zunder.tx: From Middle High German zunder, from Old High German *zuntar, zuntra, from Proto-West Germanic *tundr, from Proto-Germanic *tundrą, *tundrǭ. Akin to Dutch tonder, English tinder, Swedish tände. Related to the verb zünden.

noun:Ziel.tx: From Middle High German zil, from Old High German zil, from Proto-West Germanic *til, from Proto-Germanic *tilą. Cognate to Old English til.

adj:zahm.tx: From Middle High German and Old High German zam.

adv:zugleich.tx: From zu- (“to, at”) + gleich (“equal, same, alike”). Compare Dutch tegelijk or Polish oraz.

noun:Zweck.tx: From Middle High German zwec, zwic (“nail, pin made of wood or iron”), from Old High German zwec, zwecki (“nail, peg”), from a root probably related to Zweig (“branch, twig”); this is supported by Kroonen, though Pfeifer is skeptical and leaves the origin open. Compare Swedish svicka, svick, svicke, Danish svik, suicke, Norwegian svikk, all borrowed from Middle Low German swick, in turn borrowed …

noun:Zwang.tx: From Middle High German twanc, from Old High German geduang, from Proto-West Germanic *þwangi, from Proto-Germanic *þwangiz, Proto-Germanic *þwanguz (“coercion, constraint, band, clamp, strap”). Cognates include: Dutch dwang, Swedish tvång, and English thong.

noun:Zitrone.tx: 15th century, from Italian citrone (older variant of cedro) as well as Middle French citron, derived from Latin citrus.

noun:Zukunft.tx: From Middle High German zuokunft, zuokumft, zuokumpft, from Old High German zuokumft. See zukommen. Cognate with Middle Low German tôkumpst (whence German Low German Tokumst, Tokunft, Tokummst), Dutch toekomst, English to-come, Saterland Frisian Toukumst.

noun:Zwirn.tx: From Middle High German zwirn, from Old High German *zwirn, from Proto-West Germanic *twiʀn. More at twine, twire.

noun:Zauber.tx: From Middle High German zouber, from Old High German zoubar, from Proto-Germanic *taubrą (“magic”). Akin to Dutch tover, Old Norse taufr. More at English tiver.

adv:ziemlich.tx: From Old High German zimilīh (“befitting”) or possibly directly from ziemen + -lich.

adj:ziemlich.tx: From Old High German zimilīh (“befitting”) or possibly directly from ziemen + -lich.

adj:zart.tx: From Middle High German zart, from Old High German zart, from Proto-West Germanic *tard (“tender”). Cognate with Middle Dutch taert (“soft, weak, effeminate”).

verb:zeichnen.tx: From Middle High German zeichenen, from Old High German zeihhanōn. Synchronically, Zeichen (“token”) + -en. Compare English token (verb).

noun:Zwitter.tx: From Middle High German zwitarn (“bastard; hermaphrodite”), from Old High German zwitarn (“bastard”). The first part is the prefix zwie- (“two-, bi-”), but the identity of the second part is unknown.

verb:zögern.tx: 16th century, standard since ca. 1700. From now obsolete zogen (“to tug, pull around”) + -ern (iterative suffix), probably after Middle Low German tȫgeren (14th c., modern Low German tögern, töcheln). The underlying verb is further from Middle High German zogen, from Old High German zogōn, from Proto-West Germanic *togōn, belonging to the root of ziehen (“to pull”).

verb:zucken.tx: From Middle High German zucken, unumlauted Upper German variant of Middle High German zücken, from Old High German zuchen, from Proto-West Germanic *tukkijan. For the Upper German blocking of umlaut by /ppf/, /tts/, /kk(x)/ confer also nutzen vs. nützen or drucken vs. drücken.

verb:zünden.tx: From Middle High German zünden, from Old High German zunden, ultimately from Proto-West Germanic *tundijan. See also Zunder. Akin to English tind, Swedish tända, Gothic 𐍄𐌰𐌽𐌳𐌾𐌰𐌽 (tandjan).

noun:Ziffer.tx: From late Middle High German zifer (“digit”), from Old French cifre, from Medieval Latin cifra, from Arabic صِفْر (ṣifr).

noun:Zeh.tx: From Middle High German zēhe, from Old High German zēha, from Proto-West Germanic *taihā, from Proto-Germanic *taihwǭ (“toe”), from Proto-Indo-European *deyḱ- (“to point out”).

noun:Zeitung.tx: From Middle Dutch tīdinge, whence is borrowed Middle High German zīdunge (West Central German), from Proto-West Germanic *tīdungu (“message”), from the verb *tīdōn (“to happen”), from Proto-West Germanic *tīdi (“time, interval”). From this the later Upper German form zītunge, and then the modern form. By surface analysis, Zeit + -ung. Compare Dutch tijding, English tiding, Swedish tidning, …

verb:zwängen.tx: From Middle High German twengen, from Old High German dwengen, probably derived from Zwang. Causative to zwingen.

noun:Zusammenschluss.tx: From zusammen- + Schluss, or from zusammenschließen.

noun:Zentrum.tx: From Late Middle High German zentrum (also zenter), from Latin centrum (“centre”), from Ancient Greek κέντρον (kéntron, “centre of a circle, thorn”).

noun:Zeitschrift.tx: From Zeit (“time”) + Schrift (“writing”), "writings of the time". Attested since the 17th century in the meaning "chronogram"; in the meaning "periodical" since around 1750.

noun:Zeuge.tx: From the verb zeugen. Cognate with Dutch getuige.

noun:Zypresse.tx: From Middle High German zipresse, zipressenboum, from Old High German cipresenboum, from Latin cypressus, cupressus, from Ancient Greek κυπάρισσος (kupárissos).

noun:Zugang.tx: From Middle High German zuoganc, from Old High German zuogang. By surface analysis, deverbal from zugehen.

noun:Zionismus.tx: Zion + -ismus. Coined by Nathan Birnbaum in 1890.

noun:Zobel.tx: From Middle High German zobel, from Old High German zobal, from Old East Slavic соболь (sobolĭ). Compare English sable, Russian со́боль (sóbolʹ).

noun:Zweifel.tx: From Middle High German zwīvel, from Old High German zwīfal, from Proto-West Germanic *twīfl n, related to root of zwei. Doublet of Doppel.

noun:Zyklon.tx: Borrowed from English cyclone, ultimately from Ancient Greek κύκλος (kúklos, “circle”).

noun:Zitadelle.tx: Borrowed from Italian cittadella with influence from French citadelle. First attested in 1453, replacing earlier Schloss, and used alongside Stadtfestung or Stadtburg.

noun:Zufall.tx: From Early New High German zuoval, a calque of Latin accidēns; see zufallen. Attested in the 15th century. Cognate with Dutch toeval.

noun:Zeremonie.tx: From Middle High German cerimōnie, from Medieval Latin ceremonia, from classical caeremōnia. At first only in ecclesiastical context; broader use since ca. 1600 after French cérémonie, which also caused the now predominant final stress.

noun:Zins.tx: From Middle High German zins (“tax, tribute, interest on a lease or rent”), from Old High German zins (“tax, tribute, interest on a lease or rent”) (for which compare Old Saxon tins, Middle Dutch tijns), from Latin cēnsus. Doublet of Zensus.

verb:zähmen.tx: From Old High German zemmen, from Proto-Germanic *tamjaną. The long vowel is due to analogy with zahm.

verb:zocken.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish צחקען (tskhoken, “to gamble”), from Hebrew שיחק / שִׂחֵק (sikhék, “to play”) or צָחַק (tsakhák, “to laugh”).

verb:zerbrechen.tx: From Middle High German zerbrëchen, ziprëchen (also as zoprëchen, zuprëchen, zurprëchen), from Old High German zibrëhhan, zirbrëhhan, from Proto-Germanic *tebrekaną, *twizbrekaną (“to break apart, break in two”), equivalent to zer- + brechen. Cognate with archaic English tobreak.

noun:Zwerchfell.tx: zwerch + Fell, where zwerch is an Upper German variant of quer (“crosswise”) preserved only in a few compounds, and Fell is used in the older sense of “hide” extended to a membrane. The sense “seat of human emotion” was acquired as a calque of Ancient Greek φρήν (phrḗn).

verb:zulassen.tx: From Middle High German zuolāȥen, from Old High German zuolāȥan, from Proto-West Germanic *tōlātan. Equivalent to zu- + lassen. Cognate with Dutch toelaten, Swedish tillåta.

adj:zufrieden.tx: Since ca. 1500, from univerbation of zu + Frieden, literally “at peace”. Likely a calque of Middle Low German tô vrēde(n), Middle Dutch te vrēden (modern Dutch tevreden), both of which date from the 13th century. Apart from the dating, this is also confirmed by the fact that the earliest High German attestations are from Hesse and the Rhineland.

noun:Zinseszins.tx: Zins (“interest”) + -es- + Zins, literally “interest of interest”. First attested in the dictionary of Kaspar von Stieler (1691), with the gloss "zins auf zins anatocismus, usura usurarum".

verb:zertifizieren.tx: From Late Latin certificare, from Latin certus. Equivalent to Zertifikat (“certificate”) + -ieren (“-ise, -ify”).

noun:Zirkel.tx: From Middle High German zirkel, from Old High German zirkil, from Latin circinus (“pair of compasses”), from Ancient Greek κίρκινος (kírkinos). The Old High German -il is due to either alteration after the Germanic tool suffix *-ilaz, or confluence with Latin circulus (“circle”); the -k- speaks in favour of the latter explanation. The sense “circle”, which appears in Middle High German, is at any …

noun:Zeugnis.tx: From Middle High German geziugnisse, ziugnisse, analyzable as zeugen (“to testify, declare”) + -nis. Cognate with Vilamovian cajgnys.

noun:Zehenspitze.tx: From the plural of Zehe (“toe”) + Spitze (“tip”).

verb:zaubern.tx: From Middle High German zoubern, from Old High German zouberōn, zoubarōn from Proto-West Germanic *taubrōn, from Proto-Germanic *taubrōną. More at Zauber; cognate with English tiver.

noun:Zähre.tx: From Middle High German zære (“tears”), plural of zār m, a Central German variant of zaher, from Old High German zahar (“tear”), from Proto-West Germanic *tahr.

noun:Zugereister.tx: Strong nominative of zugereist, past participle of zureisen.

verb:zwingen.tx: From Middle High German twingen, from Old High German dwingan, from Proto-Germanic *þwinganą, *þwinhaną. Cognates include Dutch dwingen, Norwegian tvinge, Swedish tvinga, Icelandic þvinga. What may be perceived as a repetition of the consonant shift (from Germanic *þ → Old High German d → Middle High German t → modern German z) is a regular development that affected most words with Old High …

verb:zirpen.tx: Onomatopoeic. Compare Dutch tjirpen and English chirp.

verb:zwitschern.tx: Variant of earlier zwitzern, from Middle High German zwitzern, from Old High German zwizzirōn, from Proto-Germanic *twitwizōną. More at twitter.

noun:Zeche.tx: From Middle High German zëche, from Old High German *zëhhôn (attested in gizëhôn (“to arrange, regulate”)), from Proto-Germanic *tēwō (“order, array”), source of Gothic 𐍄𐌴𐍅𐌰 (tēwa), perhaps with influence from *teuhaną (“to pull”). Related to German zechen, Middle High German zechen, Old High German zehōn, Old English tēohhian, tiohhian (“to arrange”), intensive variants of German ziehen, Middle …

noun:Zeile.tx: From Middle High German zīl(e), from Old High German zīla. Outside of High German only attested in eastern Dutch tijl and Westphalian Low German Tile (both “row of sheaves”), but probably inherited from Proto-Germanic, from Proto-Indo-European *deh₂y- (“to divide”). Related with Zeit and English time.

adv:zunächst.tx: From Middle High German ze næhste (“close, directly next”). Equivalent to zu + nächst. The sense “first” developed because from the perspective of the start the next thing to do is the first thing.

noun:Zeiger.tx: From Middle High German zeiger, from Old High German zeigāri. By surface analysis, zeigen (“to show, point”) + -er. In the computing sense, a semantic loan from English pointer.

noun:Zement.tx: From Middle High German cē̆ment, byform of more common cī̆ment(e), z-, from Old French ciment, cement, from Latin caementum.

noun:Zündholz.tx: From zünden (“to light”) + Holz (“(piece of) wood”).

adj:zimperlich.tx: Cognate with Middle Dutch zimperlije, English simper.

noun:Zauberstab.tx: 16th century, from Zauber (“magic”) and/or zaubern (“to perform magic”) + Stab (“staff, wand”).

adj:zornig.tx: From Middle High German zornec, from Old High German zornag; analysable as Zorn (“anger”) + -ig.

noun:Zuschauer.tx: From Middle High German zuoschouwe. Equivalent to zuschauen + -er.

verb:zuschauen.tx: From Middle High German zuoschouwen. Equivalent to zu- + schauen.

noun:Zander.tx: From Middle Low German sandāt, from a Slavic language, from Proto-Slavic *sǫdakъ.

adj:zäh.tx: From Middle High German zǣhe, from Old High German zāhi, zāh, from Proto-West Germanic *tą̄h(ī) (“fitting; clinging; tenacious; tough”). Cognate with Dutch taai (“tough; chewy”), Low German taag (“tough; chewy”), English tough. Doublet of taff.

verb:zieren.tx: From Middle High German zieren, from Old High German ziarōn, from Proto-West Germanic *tiarī (“neat, splendid”), a formation related to Proto-Germanic *tairiz (“clear”) (whence Old Norse tærr (“clear (water)”)) and perhaps Lithuanian dyrė́ti (“to look”).

noun:Zirkon.tx: Coined by German geologist Abraham Gottlob Werner in the early 1780s on the basis of Arabic زَرْقُون (zarqūn).

verb:zwinkern.tx: From Middle High German zwinken (“to blink; twinkle”) + -ern (iterative suffix), of uncertain ultimate origin, but possibly ultimately imitative. Cognate with Middle English twinken (“to blink; twinkle”). More at English twink.

verb:zumuten.tx: From Middle High German zuomuoten. Equivalent to zu- + muten.

noun:Zinne.tx: From Middle High German zinne, from Old High German zinna, from Proto-Germanic *tindijō (“point, peak, pinnacle”), from Proto-Indo-European *h₃dónts (“tooth”). Cognate with Dutch tinne, German Low German Tinne. Related also to Old English tind (“peg, spike, prong”). More at English tine. Alternatively, Old High German zinna may descend from Proto-Germanic *tinnō, *tinnǭ, from Proto-Indo-European …

verb:zürnen.tx: From Middle High German zürnen, from Old High German zurnen.

noun:Zustand.tx: Derived from zustehen, equivalent to zu- + Stand.

noun:Zöllner.tx: From Middle High German zolnære, from Old High German zolōnāri, borrowed from Medieval Latin telonarius, from telōnium (“tollbooth”).

verb:zweifeln.tx: From Middle High German zwīvelen, zwīveln, zwībelen, from Old High German zwīfalen, zwīfalōn, from Proto-West Germanic *twīflijan, *twīflōn, from Proto-Germanic *twīflijaną. Equivalent to Zweifel + -n.

noun:Zugabe.tx: From zu- + Gabe, literally “addition” (cf. zugeben and geben).

intj:Zugabe.tx: From zu- + Gabe, literally “addition” (cf. zugeben and geben).

adj:zyklisch.tx: Borrowed from Latin cyclicus, from Ancient Greek κυκλικός (kuklikós) + -isch.

adj:zaghaft.tx: From Middle High German zaghaft, zagehaft. By surface analysis, zagen + -haft.

verb:zuschreiben.tx: Formally from Middle High German zuoschrīben (“to assure in written; to report”), from Old High German zuoscrīban (“to add in written”). Equivalent to zu- + schreiben. The modern sense emerged in the 16th century.

noun:Zuversicht.tx: From Middle High German zuofirsiht, from Old High German zuofirsiht, synchronically analyzed as zu- + ver- + Sicht.

verb:zapfen.tx: From Middle High German zapfen, from Old High German *zapfōn, from Proto-West Germanic *tappōn, from Proto-Germanic *tappōną. Cognate with Dutch tappen, German Low German tappen, English tap.

noun:Zusammenstoß.tx: Deverbal from zusammenstoßen. By surface analysis, zusammen (“together”) + Stoß (“push, shove, bump”)

noun:Zettel.tx: From Early New High German zeddel, zedel, from Middle High German zëdele, zëdel, a loan from Italian cedola, from Medieval Latin cedula, schedula, the diminutive of scheda, scida (“strip of papyrus”) ultimately from Ancient Greek σχίδη (skhídē, “splinter, fragment”). Cognate to Low German Zeddel, Palatine Rhine Franconian Zeddel, English schedule. The spelling with -tt- was found from the 15th …

verb:zusammenziehen.tx: From Middle High German zesamenziehen, zesameneziehen. Equivalent to zusammen- + ziehen.

adj:zivil.tx: From French civil, from Latin cīvīlis. [from 16th c.]

noun:Zivil.tx: From French civil, from Latin civīlis.

adv:zweifelsohne.tx: Univerbation of Zweifels (“of doubt”) + ohne (“without”), from Middle High German zwīvels āne, during which ohne could still take a genitive object: "einer Sache ohne sein".

adv:zuletzt.tx: zu + letzter; cognate with Hunsrik zuletst

verb:zugeben.tx: From Middle High German zuogeben, from Old High German zuogeban. Equivalent to zu- + geben.

verb:zurren.tx: From Low German sorren, *zorren, perhaps from Dutch tsorren, older variant of sjorren. Further origin uncertain.

verb:züchten.tx: From Middle High German zühten, from Old High German zuhten (“rear, nourish”). By surface analysis, Zucht (“breeding”) + -en (“verbal suffix”).

adj:zinnen.tx: From Middle High German zinīn, from Old High German zinīn. Equivalent to Zinn + -en; cognates include obsolete English tinnen.

noun:Zelot.tx: Borrowed from Latin zēlōtēs, from Ancient Greek ζηλωτής (zēlōtḗs). See zealot.

noun:Zilpzalp.tx: Echoic of the bird’s song; compare English chiffchaff.

noun:Zepter.tx: Middle High German zepter, cepter, scepter, from Latin scēptrum.

verb:zeugen.tx: From Middle High German ziugen, geziugen, from Old High German giziugon, from ziug, ultimately from the root of ziehen (“to move, pull, migrate”). Equivalent to Zeug + -en. Cognate with Vilamovian cajgia.

verb:zumachen.tx: From Middle High German zuomachen, zuo machen, zūmachen, equivalent to zu- + machen. Compare Middle Low German tômaken, whence German Low German tomaken.

noun:Zwietracht.tx: From Middle High German zwitraht, which is a borrowing and phonetic adaptation from Middle Low German twēdraht.

verb:zerren.tx: From Middle High German zerren, from Old High German zerren, from Proto-Germanic *tarjaną, and hence a doublet of German zehren, which see for the ultimate source. The geminated -rr- is irregular and probably intensive (compare the same in Middle Low German terren, Middle Dutch terren, both alongside tēren). Compare English tear.

noun:Zusammenkunft.tx: Verbal noun of zusammenkommen, with Kunft.

noun:Zagel.tx: From Middle High German zagel, from Old High German zagal, from Proto-West Germanic *tagl, from Proto-Germanic *taglą. Cognate with English tail.

noun:Zentner.tx: Ultimately from Latin centēnārius (“containing hundred”), from centum (“hundred”)

prep:zugunsten.tx: Univerbation of zu + Gunsten, from Gunst (“favor”).

adv:zwar.tx: From Middle High German zwāre, contraction of ze wāre (“verily, indeed”), from Old High German zi wāre (8th c.). Equivalent to zu + wahr. The concessive use developed first in cognate Middle Low German twâre. Compare Czech sice.

noun:Zügel.tx: From Middle High German zügel, zugel, from Old High German zugil, from Proto-Germanic *tugilaz (“rein on a horse”), whence also Old Norse tygill, Old English tigel, Dutch teugel. Ultimately derives from Proto-Indo-European *dewk-.

noun:Zentrifuge.tx: 19th century, from New Latin centrifuga, feminine of centrifugus (“centrifugal”).

noun:Zwielicht.tx: Calque of German Low German Tweelicht, from Middle Low German twêlicht, equivalent to zwie- + Licht. Compare Dutch tweelicht, English twilight.

adv:zweierlei.tx: From Middle High German zweierleie, zweigerleie, equivalent to zwei + -erlei.

noun:Zeder.tx: From Middle High German zēder, cēder, from Old High German cēdar, from Latin cedrus, from Ancient Greek κέδρος (kédros).

verb:zappeln.tx: From Late Middle High German zappel(e)n (15th c.), from older zabel(e)n, from Old High German zabalōn (“to move, wriggle”), from Proto-West Germanic *tabulōn, from Proto-Germanic *tablōną, an iterative-diminutive of Proto-Germanic *tabōną, whence English tave (“to struggle, wrestle”). Ultimately onomatopoeic, like younger tappen. In zab(b)eln, the short vowel was preserved under the influence of …

noun:Zehnt.tx: From Middle High German zehent, zehente, zehnde, zehende, from Old High German zehanto (“tenth, tithe”), from Proto-West Germanic *tehundō, from Proto-Germanic *tehundô (“tenth”). Cognate with German Low German Teihnte, Dutch tiende, English tithe.

verb:zügeln.tx: Perhaps from Zügel. Cognate with Alemannic German zügle.

noun:Ziegenbock.tx: From Middle High German zigenboc, equivalent to Ziege + -n- + Bock. Compare German Low German Zegenbuck.

noun:Zensus.tx: From Latin census. Doublet of Zins.

verb:zugehen.tx: From Middle High German zuogān, zuogēn, from Old High German zuogān, zuogēn. Equivalent to zu- + gehen.

noun:Zarge.tx: From Middle High German zarge (“side wall, frame, embankment”), from Old High German zarga (“rim, side wall”), from Proto-West Germanic *targā, from Proto-Germanic *targǭ (“edge”), from Proto-Indo-European *derǵʰ- (“to catch, grasp”). Cognate with Old Norse targa (“small shield”) and thence English targe.

noun:Zytoplasma.tx: Coined by Albert von Kölliker in 1863.

noun:Zimmermann.tx: From Middle High German zimberman, zimmerman, zimerman, from Old High German zimbarman. Equivalent to Zimmer (“timber”) (obsolete sense) + Mann (“man”). The surname is an occupational one, derived from the noun. Piecewise cognate of Dutch timmerman, Swedish timmerman, Norwegian Bokmål tømmermann, English timberman.

verb:zerstäuben.tx: From Middle High German zerstouben, from Old High German zistouben. Equivalent to zer- + stäuben.

noun:Zöliakie.tx: From New Latin coeliacia, from Latin coeliacus (“relating to the abdomen”).

phrase:zwei Dumme, ein Gedanke.tx: Literally, “two fools, one thought”. Likely a sarcastic alteration of the now rarer variant zwei Seelen, ein Gedanke (literally “two souls, one thought”).

noun:Zinnober.tx: From Middle High German zinober, from Old French cinobre, from Latin cinnabaris, from Ancient Greek κιννάβαρι (kinnábari).

num:zehnte.tx: From Middle High German zëhente, from Old High German zehanto, from Proto-West Germanic *tehundō, from Proto-Germanic *tehundô. Equivalent to zehn + -te.

adj:zwölfte.tx: From Middle High German zwelfte, from Old High German zwelifto, from Proto-Germanic *twaliftô. Equivalent to zwölf + -te.

noun:Zucht.tx: From Middle High German zuht, from Old High German zuht, from Proto-Germanic *tuhtiz (“discipline, pulling”). Cognate with Saterland Frisian Tucht.

noun:Zählung.tx: From the verb zählen, + -ung. Attested since the 17th century.

verb:zecken.tx: From Middle High German zecken, Old High German zechōn, from Proto-West Germanic *tikkōn (“to touch, tap”), perhaps originally of onomatopoeic origin. Compare Luxembourgish zecken, English tick, Italian azzeccare (“to hit”).

adj:zünftig.tx: Inherited from Middle High German zünftic, from Old High German zumftīg. Equivalent to Zunft (“guild of craftsmen”) + -ig.

verb:zanken.tx: From late Middle High German zanken, of unclear origin, not having been recorded in earlier periods. Perhaps from the root of Zinke (“prong, sharp point”), if the original sense was "to be pointed."

verb:zufügen.tx: zu- + fügen. Compare with Danish tilføje, Dutch toevoegen.

noun:Zacke.tx: From Middle High German zacke, from Old High German *zacho, from Proto-West Germanic *takkō (“twig, branch, shoot”). Cognate with Dutch tak (“branch”), English tack.

noun:Zehntel.tx: From Middle High German zehenteil. Equivalent to zehn + Teil.

verb:zerlegen.tx: From Middle High German zerlegen. Equivalent to zer- + legen.

adv:zueinander.tx: From Middle High German zuoeinander. Equivalent to zu- + einander.

pt: to allow, to permit; to license
noun:Zulassung.tx: From zulassen (“to allow, to permit; to license”) + -ung (“-ing”). Compare Dutch toelating.

adj:zehnfach.tx: From Middle High German zehenvach, equivalent to Zehn + -fach.

adj:zeitlich.tx: From Middle High German zītlīch, from Old High German zītlīhho, equivalent to Zeit + -lich. Compare English tidely.

verb:zusagen.tx: From Middle High German zuosagen. Equivalent to zu- + sagen.

noun:Zoch.tx: From Ripuarian Central Franconian Zoch, a cognate and synonym of standard German Zug (which see).

noun:Zunft.tx: From Middle High German zunft, Old High German zumft, from Proto-Germanic *tumþiz (“guild”). Equivalent to an abstract verbal noun of ziemen; compare Kunft from kommen.

noun:Ziegler.tx: From Middle High German ziegeler. Equivalent to Ziegel + -er.

verb:zeihen.tx: From Middle High German zīhen, from Old High German zīhan, from Proto-West Germanic *tīhan. See also zeigen.

noun:Zusammenbruch.tx: Deverbal from zusammenbrechen, equivalent to zusammen- + Bruch.

noun:Zain.tx: From Middle High German zein, from Old High German zein, from Proto-West Germanic *tain (“rod”). Cognate with English mistletoe.

adj:zappenduster.tx: Compound of Zappen (“cone”) + duster (“dark”). The first component points to Zapfenstreich (“curfew, last post”), but may also be based on Hebrew צָפוֹן (tsafón, “north, hence midnight”). Both words have probably contributed, it being unknown which is original and which secondary.

verb:zusammenfallen.tx: From Middle High German zesamenvallen, zesamenevallen, from Old High German zisamanefallan. Equivalent to zusammen- + fallen. In the sense “to merge” probably a calque of Latin coincidēre.

verb:zuziehen.tx: From Middle High German zuoziehen, from Old High German zuoziohan. Analysable as zu (“to; shut”) + ziehen (“pull, move”).

verb:zacken.tx: From Middle High German zacke, from Old High German *zacho, from Proto-West Germanic *takkō (“twig, branch, shoot”).

noun:Zuflucht.tx: From Middle High German zuovluht, from Old High German zuofluht. Equivalent to zu- + Flucht (“escape”).

verb:zerdeppern.tx: Probably from a Central German form of Topf (“pot”). Compare Luxembourgish Dëppen.

verb:zerrütten.tx: From Middle High German zerrütten, ultimately from the root of rütteln (“to jolt, shake”).

adv:zeitlebens.tx: Univerbation of zeit + Lebens, merged in writing since the late 17th century, from earlier (and still extant) zeit jemandes Lebens.

verb:zetteln.tx: Attested in Upper and Central German from the 15th century, zetteln is an l-diminutive of the verb zetten (“scatter, strew”) (a cognate of Old Norse teðja (“to scatter manure”)), from Proto-Germanic *tadjaną (“to strew, scatter”), whence also dialectal English tath (“dung”). Grimm suspects that the technical meaning "to warp the loom" (also 15th century) is derived via the noun Zettel (“warp”) …

noun:Zier.tx: From Middle High German ziere, from Old High German ziari. See zieren (“to decorate”).

verb:zehren.tx: From Middle High German zern, zeren, from Old High German zeren, from Proto-Germanic *tarjaną, partly merged in Middle High German with related Old High German zeran, from Proto-Germanic *teraną. Cognate with Dutch teren and, through *teraną, with English tear (“rip, rend”).

verb:zwicken.tx: From Middle High German zwicken (“to fasten with nails, squeeze in, pinch, tug”), Old High German *zwicchēn, from Proto-West Germanic *twikkijan (“to nail, pin, fasten, clasp, pinch”). Cognate with Middle English twicchen (whence English twitch), Low German twikken.

verb:zerreißen.tx: From Middle High German zerrīȥen, zer- + reißen.

verb:zusammenfügen.tx: From Middle High German zesamenvüegen, zesamenevüegen, zesamenvuogen, from Old High German zisamanefuogen, zisamanafuogen. Equivalent to zusammen- + fügen.

noun:Zauberspruch.tx: Zauber (“magic, enchantment”) + Spruch (“quote, medieval lyric poem”).

noun:Zwist.tx: From rare Middle High German zwist (Ripuarian, 14th c.), borrowed from Middle Dutch twist, from Proto-West Germanic *twist, from Proto-Germanic *twistaz (whence also English twist). Later reinforced by cognate Low German Twist, from Middle Low German twist, twest. Since ca. 1700 in regular standard usage, where it remained an elevated word, however. Related to zwei (as in Zwietracht). Doublet of Twist.

noun:Zärtlichkeit.tx: From late Middle High German zertlīcheit. By surface analysis, zärtlich + -keit.

noun:Zank.tx: Back-formation from zanken (“to row, to squabble”).

noun:Zuhause.tx: Substantive of zuhause, alternative form of zu Hause (“at home”).

noun:Zwickmühle.tx: Alteration of older Fickmühle, a compound of ficken + Mühle, in which ficken is used in the archaic sense of “to slide”. The alteration was without doubt driven by the need to avoid the vulgar verb. Formally it may be due to conflation with an unattested *Zwiemühle from zwie- (“double”), as well as to association with zwicken (“to pinch”).

adj:zeitig.tx: From Middle High German zītec, from Old High German zītig. Equivalent to Zeit (“time”) + -ig. Cognate with Dutch tijdig, English tidy. For the sense “early” compare Czech časný.

verb:zetern.tx: From Middle High German zēter, originally an interjection to ask for help when being robbed or attacked which, per Törnquist, comes from ze æhte her.

verb:zusammenbinden.tx: From Middle High German zesamenbinden, zesamenebinden, from Old High German zisamanebintan. Equivalent to zusammen- + binden.

noun:Zweisamkeit.tx: Originally jocular, derived from Einsamkeit (“solitude, loneliness”) by replacing ein (“one”) with zwei (“two”). Compare Dutch tweezaamheid (possibly after the German).

adv:zwischendurch.tx: Equivalent to zwischen (“between”) + durch (“through”). Compare Dutch tussendoor.

verb:zertreten.tx: From Middle High German zertreten, from Old High German zitretan. Equivalent to zer- + treten.

noun:Zeller.tx: Dialectal byform. See the lemma for more.

noun:Zimmerer.tx: The noun is from Zimmer + -er. The surname is an occupational one, from the noun.

noun:Zwille.tx: Sporadically since the 16th century, regular use since the later 20th century. From Low German Twill, Twille, Twele, from Middle Low German twil (“crotch”), from Proto-Germanic *twizlaz, *twizlō, whence also Dutch twil (“kind of lath used in shipbuilding”). Alongside Proto-Germanic *twislaz, *twislō, whence the German doublet Zwiesel and Old English twisla (“bifurcation of a river”). The form …

verb:zustellen.tx: From zu- + stellen. Compare Dutch toestellen.

noun:Zauberwürfel.tx: From Zauber (“magic”) + Würfel (“die, cube”), calque of Hungarian bűvös kocka.

noun:Zofe.tx: 17th century, from East Central German dialects. Earlier already Zoffmagd (16th c.). Pertaining to a group of (probably interrelated) verbs zoffen, zaffen (“to hesitate”), zaufen (“to step back, walk behind”), Middle High German zāven (“to pull, rear, groom”). Which form exactly underlies seems uncertain; Middle High German -o-, -ou-, -ā- could all have become [oː] in the dialects in question. …

verb:ziemen.tx: From Middle High German zëmen, Old High German zëman. Cognate with Old Saxon tëman (archaic English teem), Dutch betamen (“to be proper, suit”), Gothic 𐌲𐌰𐍄𐌹𐌼𐌰𐌽 (gatiman).

verb:zuteilen.tx: From Middle High German zuoteilen. Equivalent to zu- + teilen.

verb:zusetzen.tx: From Middle High German zuosetzen. Analysable as zu- (“to, at”) + setzen (“to set, put”).

verb:zermürben.tx: From Middle High German zermürfen, analyzable as zer- + mürbe + -en.

verb:zaudern.tx: Uncertain. Perhaps related to Dutch toeven (“to linger”).

verb:zuschieben.tx: From Middle High German zuoschīben (“to aid, to assist”). Equivalent to zu- + schieben.

adj:zuvorkommend.tx: Literally, “pre-empting, acting in advance”, thus in the idiomatic sense “helpful without the need to ask”.

verb:zimmern.tx: From Middle High German zimbern, from Old High German zimbren, zimbarōn, from Proto-Germanic *timrijaną, derived from *timrą, whence German Zimmer. Cognate with Dutch timmeren, English timber.

pt: to commit or admit to an institution
verb:zwangseinweisen.tx: From Zwang (“compulsion”) + einweisen (“to commit or admit to an institution”). Probably denominal after Zwangseinweisung.

verb:zerfleddern.tx: Late 18th century, of dialectal, especially East Central German, origin, from zer- + fled(d)ern, the latter from Middle High German vlëderen (“to flutter”), related with flattern, Fledermaus. The form with -dd- may be expressive or due to shortening before -er- (as in Hammer, Mutter, Widder etc.).

noun:Zukunftsmusik.tx: Zukunft + -s- + Musik, “music of the future”. Initially coined as term of abuse for Richard Wagner's music by Ludwig Bischoff in the 1850s., the original sense being "music that will only find appreciation in the future". As a metaphor for non-musical plans and ideas, it occurs as early as the 1890s.

noun:Zollstock.tx: 18th century, from Zoll (“inch”) + Stock (“stick”). Compare equivalent Dutch duimstok.

adj:zweischneidig.tx: From zwei + Schneide + -ig. Compare Middle High German zweisnīderic, zweisnīdric (“two-edged”).

verb:zerbersten.tx: From Middle High German zerbresten, from Old High German zirbrestan, zibrestan. Equivalent to zer- + bersten.

adv:zuhauf.tx: Univerbation of zu + Hauf. The latter is an old stem variant of Haufen (“pile”). Compare Low German tohoop, Dutch tehoop.

noun:Zeitenwende.tx: From Zeit + -en- + Wende. Compare Dutch tijdwende.

noun:Zille.tx: From Middle High German zülle, probably ultimately from Proto-Slavic *čьlnъ. Doublet of Schinakel. Compare Bavarian Zün.

noun:Zierde.tx: From Middle High German zierde, from Old High German zierida. Equivalent to obsolete zier (“splendid, glorious”) + -de (“-th, -ness”).

verb:zwacken.tx: From Middle High German zwacken, an imitative alteration of zwicken.

verb:zollen.tx: From Middle High German zollen. Equivalent to Zoll + -en.

verb:zäumen.tx: From Middle High German zöumen, zoumen.

verb:zücken.tx: From Middle High German zücken, from Old High German zucken, zuhhen, from Proto-West Germanic *tukkijan.

noun:Zimbel.tx: From Latin cymbalum, from Ancient Greek κύμβαλον (kúmbalon). Doublet of Zimbal.

verb:zweckentfremden.tx: From the expression etwas seinem Zweck entfremden (literally “to alienate something from its purpose”). Historically, either from Zweck + entfremden or by backformation from Zweckentfremdung.

verb:zubringen.tx: From Middle High German zuobringen, from Old High German zuobringan. Equivalent to zu- + bringen.

noun:Ziborium.tx: Borrowed from Latin cibōrium, from Ancient Greek κιβώριον (kibṓrion).

verb:zahnen.tx: The verb is attested since the 16th century and can be compared with Old High German zennen.

noun:Zuckerhut.tx: Zucker (“sugar”) + Hut (“hat”). Attested since the 18th century.

verb:zerschneiden.tx: From Middle High German zersnīden, from Old High German zasnīdan. By surface analysis, zer- + schneiden.

phrase:zu Urkund dessen.tx: Compare French en foi de quoi, sur foi de quoi.

noun:Zappelphilipp.tx: zappeln + Philipp. Coined by Heinrich Hoffmann in his 1845 children's book Der Struwwelpeter.

noun:Zuschnitt.tx: Deverbal from zuschneiden, equivalent to zu- + Schnitt.

noun:Zwinge.tx: From Middle High German twenge and Middle Low German dwenge (“constraint, clamp; lace”), from Proto-Germanic *þwanguz, *þwangiz, cognate with English thong, German Zwang. Derived from the root in Middle High German twengen (“to squeeze, force, cram”) (> modern German zwängen) and Middle Low German dwengen (“to squeeze, press”). Cognate with Old Norse þvengr, Danish tvinge.

noun:Ziesel.tx: From Middle High German zisel, probably ultimately from Proto-Slavic *sysьlъ. Forms ending in Maus (“mouse”) were formerly more common: Old High German zisimūs, Middle High German zisemūs, and German Zieselmaus.

noun:Zungenschlag.tx: From Zunge (“tongue”) + -n- + Schlag (“hit, slap”). Compare Dutch tongval.

noun:Zosse.tx: 18th century, spread from Berlin. Borrowed from Yiddish סוס (sus), from Hebrew סוס (sūs). Initial [s] is a (now dated) allophone of /t͡s/ in Berlin and other parts of northern Germany; hence the z-spelling.

noun:Zisterzienser.tx: Zisterz + -i- + -enser, a calque of Latin Cisterciensis, from Latin Cistercium (“Cîteaux”), after the place where the order was founded.

noun:Ziestag.tx: Middle High German ziestac, from Old High German ziestag, ciesdac, from Proto-West Germanic *Tīwas dag (literally “Tiw's day”), a calque of Latin diēs Mārtis (literally “day of Mars”). Cognate with English Tuesday, West Frisian tiisdei, Swedish tisdag.

noun:Zeisig.tx: From Middle High German zīsec, zīsic. Cognate with Czech čížek (“siskin”). Ultimately from Proto-Slavic *čižь.

noun:Zierrat.tx: From Middle High German zierōt, derived from Middle High German ziere (and its ancestral forms) and the Germanic suffix *-ōd(i)-, expressing a state or condition (cf. Heimat). As the suffix is archaic in modern German, the word is usually reinterpreted as a compound of Zier (“decoration”) and Rat (“goods, effects”) and spelled accordingly. The Duden dictionary lists the latter as the dominant form.

noun:Zerberus.tx: Borrowed from Latin Cerberus, from Ancient Greek Κέρβερος (Kérberos).

adv:zunichte.tx: From Middle High German ze nihte (“to nothing”).

verb:zusammenbringen.tx: From Middle High German zesamenbringen, zesamenebringen, from Old High German zisamanebringan. Equivalent to zusammen- + bringen.

noun:Zuvorkommenheit.tx: From zuvorkommend + -heit. The elision of the d is regular, cf. Abwesenheit, Unwissenheit etc.

phrase:zwischen Baum und Borke.tx: Literally, “between tree and bark”. Compare French entre l'arbre et l'écorce

verb:zubinden.tx: From Middle High German zuobinden. Equivalent to zu- + binden.

noun:Zvieri.tx: From Alemannic German Zvieri, z'Vieri, from zue (“at”) and vier (“four”).

verb:zähnen.tx: From Middle High German zenen, zennen, zenden, from Old High German zenen, zennen, zenden, from Proto-West Germanic *tanþijan. Cognate with Middle Low German tēnen, English teethe.

verb:zuwachsen.tx: From Middle High German zuowahsen. By surface analysis, zu- + wachsen

noun:Zampano.tx: From Italian Zampanò, name of a character in the 1954 film La Strada.

phrase:Zahl oder Ähre.tx: Literally, “number or ear of corn”. The symbol on the back of the Pfennig coins did not represent ears of corn, but oak leaves. Ears of corn were in fact shown on the number side (around the number). However, the backs of some older Pfennig coins (e.g. in the Weimar Republic) had ears on them, and the phrase must go back to that time.

noun:Zottel.tx: Attested 15th century, perhaps older. Equivalent to Zotte + -el (diminutive suffix).

verb:zicken.tx: From Middle High German zicken (“to bicker, push, tease”), related to Middle High German zic (“a tap, nudge; teasing, malicious act”). Perhaps a variant of Middle High German zecken (“to tap, nudge”), from Old High German zehhōn (“to stimulate, incite”), from Proto-West Germanic *tikkōn (“to tap, nudge”). Alternatively, perhaps derived from Middle High German zickīn (“young goat, kid”), from Old …

noun:Zuckerfest.tx: From Zucker (“sugar”) + Fest (“feast, holiday”), a calque of Turkish Şeker Bayramı.

verb:zwiebeln.tx: 17th century, from Zwiebel (“onion”) + -n. Some of the early attestations suggest that the underlying notion is that of a gradual ridding or wearing down, thus based on the way onions can be peeled layer by layer. Alternatively it might be from the sharpness to the taste and the irritancy to the eyes.

noun:Zweckentfremdung.tx: From the expression etwas seinem Zweck entfremden (literally “to alienate something from its purpose”). Historically, either from zweckentfremden + -ung or from Zweck + Entfremdung.

noun:Zores.tx: Borrowed from Yiddish צרות (tsores), plural of צרה (tsore, “trouble, problem”), from Hebrew צָרָה (tsará, “trouble, tragedy, calamity”).

noun:Zeremonienmeister.tx: From Zeremonie + -n- + Meister. The word preserves an older stress pattern of the first component.

verb:zweigen.tx: From Middle High German zwîgen, from Old High German zwîgen. By surface analysis, Zweig + -en.

verb:zuzeln.tx: From Bavarian zuzln, possibly from onomatopoetic origin.

noun:Zichorie.tx: From Italian cicoria, from Medieval Latin or Late Latin *cichōria, from the plural of Latin cichorium, from Ancient Greek κιχώριον (kikhṓrion). Doublet of Chicorée.

noun:Zephir.tx: Borrowed from Latin Zephyrus, from Ancient Greek Ζέφυρος (Zéphuros, “Zephyrus, the west wind”).

adj:zeremoniell.tx: By surface analysis, Zeremonie + -ell. Borrowed from French cérémoniel.

noun:Zerstäuber.tx: 17th century, derived from zerstäuben. The sense of nebulizer developed in the 19th century.

verb:zerspalten.tx: From Middle High German zerspalten, from Old High German zirspaltan, zispaltan. Equivalent to zer- + spalten.

verb:zureiten.tx: From Middle High German zuorīten, from Old High German zuorītan. Equivalent to zu- + reiten.

verb:zuhalten.tx: From Middle High German zuohalten. Equivalent to zu- + halten.

verb:zureden.tx: From Middle High German zuoreden. Equivalent to zu- + reden.

pt: anything used for lighting a fire
noun:Zigarettenanzünder.tx: From Zigarette (“cigarette”) + -n- + Anzünder (“anything used for lighting a fire”).

noun:Zweifler.tx: From Middle High German zwīvelære, from Old High German zwīvalāri, zwīfalāri. By surface analysis, zweifeln + er.

noun:Zauberbuch.tx: From zaubern (“to conjure, to perform magic”) + Buch (“book”).

phrase:zwei Seelen, ein Gedanke.tx: Literally, “two souls, one thought”. Likely a humorous application of the verse Zwei Seelen, ein Gedanke / Zwei Herzen und ein Schlag (“Two souls, one thought / Two hearts and one beat”) from the romantic drama Der Sohn der Wildnis (“The Son of the Wilderness”) by Austrian dramatist Friedrich Halm (1842).

verb:zwirbeln.tx: From Middle High German zwirbeln, which an intensivation of zwirben (“turn around”). Probably related to Wirbel (“whirl”). See also twirl.

adj:zutraulich.tx: From zutrauen + -lich. The verb is used here in the archaic sense of “to trust” (German vertrauen). Compare vertraulich, which however has a somewhat different sense.

verb:zäunen.tx: From Middle High German ziunen, zūnen, from Old High German zūnen, from Proto-West Germanic tūnijan.

noun:Zielwasser.tx: zielen (“to aim”) + Wasser (“water”), from the idea of alcohol improving and steadying one's aim. First used in the late 19th century in contexts such as hunting, though Küpper claims that it was previously used to refer to drinks taken as a punishment for missing in shooting competitions. Initially referred to actual beverages, but also gained purely metaphorical usage to comment on one's aim by the 20th century.
